source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (rev. 2024) Fallacies; on Hamblin (1970) Fallacies
finding: Hamblin's 1970 book was the first modern book-length attack on the textbook 'standard treatment' of fallacies (Copi 1961 as target). He set out the standard definition: a fallacy is an argument that seems valid but is not. He asked for dialectical rules, not only formal logic. Hansen (2002) showed Hamblin overstated how widely that definition was held.
numbers: Three conditions in the standard definition: argument, invalidity, appearance. The post-Hamblin era of fallacy studies starts in the 1970s.
quote: debased, worn-out and dogmatic a treatment as could be imagined
limits: Read through the SEP summary, not Hamblin's book itself (not online). Hamblin's historical claim is disputed by Hansen.
agent_relevance: Our agent should not treat a fallacy label as proof of a bad claim. A label only says the support is defective.

source: SEP Fallacies; Massey (1981) asymmetry thesis
finding: Massey argued there is no systematic theory of invalidity. You can show validity by form, but you cannot show invalidity by pointing to an invalid form. So under the standard definition no argument can be convicted of being a fallacy on logical grounds alone.
numbers: No numbers. One argument, one asymmetry.
limits: Philosophical argument; contested.
agent_relevance: Supports a design rule: do not decide 'fallacy' from surface form. Use a check that tests support (see critical questions in a20).

source: SEP Fallacies; Woods and Walton (1989) / Woods (1992) methodological pluralism
finding: Woods and Walton said formal logic is too coarse for most fallacies and matched each to a fitting logic: inductive logic (hasty generalization, post hoc), relatedness logic (ignoratio elenchi), plausible-reasoning theory (ad verecundiam), dialectical game theory (begging the question, many questions). Woods called this methodological pluralism. Later he argued the implicit fallacy 'rules' work as heuristic directives.
numbers: Four fallacy-to-logic pairings named.
limits: Theory only; no test of whether the matched logics predict human or model judgments.
agent_relevance: A fallacy checker is several small checkers (a source check, a causal check, a scope check), not one detector. This fits our code-checked guardrails.

source: Walton (1995) A Pragmatic Theory of Fallacy, as summarised in SEP Fallacies
finding: Walton's pragmatic theory: arguments are judged inside a type of dialogue (persuasion, inquiry, negotiation, eristic and others). In 1995 he said a fallacy occurs on an illicit shift from one dialogue type to another. He later moved away from that as the sole explanation. His monographs cover begging the question (1991), slippery slope (1992), ad hominem (1998).
numbers: Walton and Krabbe (1995) / Walton (2007) list seven dialogue types. The SEP informal-logic entry notes that in eristic dialogue threats and insults can be permissible.
limits: Secondary summary. The dialogue-shift account was later weakened by Walton himself.
agent_relevance: Same words can be fine in one task and an error in another. The agent should tag which dialogue it is in (information seeking vs persuasion) before flagging an authority or a guess.

source: van Eemeren and Grootendorst (1984, 1992, 2004) pragma-dialectics, as summarised in SEP Fallacies
finding: In pragma-dialectics a fallacy is any violation of one of ten rules for a critical discussion across four stages (confrontation, opening, argumentation, concluding). Fallacies need not be arguments, the invalidity condition is dropped, and the 'appears sound' condition is dropped as too subjective. Strategic maneuvering that derails is a fallacy. New fallacies appear, such as declaring a standpoint sacrosanct and evading the burden of proof.
numbers: 10 rules; 4 stages. The 2004 text: every violation of the rules is a fallacy.
quote: every violation of any of the rules of the discussion procedure
limits: The rules are the theorists' ideal; whether ordinary arguers accept them is an empirical question (see a06-a07).
agent_relevance: Maps well to a move-level checker: 'burden of proof evaded', 'standpoint made untouchable' are checkable moves, not form tests.

source: van Eemeren, Meuffels, Verburg (2000) and ISSA 2002 report: conventional validity of the pragma-dialectical freedom rule (Dutch pupils, six experiments)
finding: Ordinary arguers rate rule-violating moves as less reasonable than sound moves. Six experiments, 7-point scale (1 very unreasonable, 7 very reasonable); each respondent rated 48 fragments (36 fallacious, 12 sound) in scientific, political, domestic settings. Direct personal attack was always rated less reasonable than tu quoque. Physical ad baculum was rated worst; tu quoque best.
numbers: Ad hominem study: fallacies 3.75 vs sound 5.29. Replication (24 respondents, 24 items): tu quoque 3.82, circumstantial 3.47, abusive 2.99; fallacies 3.43 vs sound 5.27. Of 170 interpretable justifications, about 86% were about argument quality, about 11% about politeness. Tu quoque in ad misericordiam-I was rated as reasonable as sound moves (the one non-significant case).
limits: Secondary page fetch; per-study N is not given there. Dutch 17-year-old pupils. Stated judgments, not behaviour. Authors say results do not generalize to real discussions.
agent_relevance: Humans do not treat all rule-breaking equally. Tu quoque and circumstantial attacks look more acceptable. Agent flags should carry a severity, not a flat 'fallacy'.

source: ISSA 2002 report: proposition-type control and Spanish replications of the freedom-rule studies
finding: Proposition type (descriptive, evaluative, inciting) had no significant effect on ratings. Spanish replications (n=47 and n=29) found the same direction but a different size: Spanish respondents did not separate domestic from scientific settings, and 33% of interpretable justifications were about politeness versus about 11% in the Dutch data.
numbers: Proposition-type study: 75 respondents (38 + 37), 72 fragments; direct/indirect/tu quoque means 3.11/3.92/4.85 (group I) and 2.88/3.76/4.26 (group II). Spain: fallacies 3.54 vs sound 4.97; direct 3.01, indirect 3.61, tu quoque 3.99; domestic 3.27, scientific 3.07, political 4.27. Of 348 Spanish justifications 41% were uninterpretable.
limits: Small samples. Politeness is a competing explanation for 'unreasonable' ratings, stronger in Spain.
agent_relevance: Culture and politeness shift what counts as an error. A flag based on tone will misfire. Use support-based checks.

source: Lillo-Unglaube, Canales-Johnson, Navarrete, Bravo (2014) Toward an experimental account of argumentation (perspective, Front. Psychol. 5:1420)
finding: Summarises two lines of fallacy experiments. Corner et al. (2011) slippery slope: similar items drove acceptance of the next item; dissimilar items did not. van Eemeren et al. (2012) ad hominem: abusive attacks were rated less unreasonable when the first speaker's authority was only implied (disguised) than when stated openly; in the disguised case the attack was rated neither reasonable nor unreasonable (7-point scale).
numbers: Stimulus example from Corner et al.: areas with 224 and 179 species. No sample sizes or statistics are given in this article.
limits: Perspective piece with no data of its own. Numbers must be taken from the original papers.
agent_relevance: Whether an attack on a source is fair depends on whether the source is really the evidence. The agent's marked authority/guess block should record how the claim leans on the source.

source: Boongaling (2016) Commentary on Lillo-Unglaube et al., Front. Psychol. 7:299
finding: Critique: Bayesian strength of slippery slope and ad hominem depends on priors, while the traditional view calls such arguments defective because the conclusion does not follow. So the experimental (psychological) and normative views are not simply merged.
numbers: No numbers. Cites Hahn and Oaksford (2007, Psychol. Rev. 114:704-732).
limits: Short commentary; no new data.
agent_relevance: The same surface argument can be strong or weak by content. Do not treat form as the verdict.

source: Hahn and Oaksford (2007) The rationality of informal argumentation: a Bayesian approach to reasoning fallacies, Psychological Review 114:704-732 (via SEP and search abstract)
finding: Bayesian account: argument strength is a probability that depends on prior belief in the claim, the evidence, and rival hypotheses. Strength runs from 0 to 1, so tokens of one fallacy type can be strong or weak. They tested three fallacies experimentally: argument from ignorance, circular argument, slippery slope. A fallacy is an argument with low probability on this model.
numbers: Three fallacy types tested. Factors: prior belief, evidence polarity, source reliability.
limits: I could not open the 2007 PDF (403). Details come from SEP and a search abstract, not the paper. Experiment numbers not captured.
agent_relevance: A probabilistic strength score fits G5 (code normalises probabilities). A flagged argument gets a weight, not a ban.

source: Bayindir, Hahn, Oaksford (2005) How convinced should we be by negative evidence? CogSci 27, Experiment 1
finding: Tests the Bayesian reading of argument from ignorance. 73 Cardiff students rated how convinced a dialogue character should be (0-10) in a 4 (topic) x 2 (polarity) x 2 (reliability) x 2 (prior belief) design. Positive arguments beat negative ones, a reliable source beat an unreliable one, strong prior beat weak prior.
numbers: Polarity: positive m=4.53 vs negative m=4.27, F(1,72)=11.58, p=.001. Reliability: m=5.58 vs 3.21, F(1,72)=198.63, p<.0001. Prior belief: m=4.47 vs 4.32, F(1,72)=5.96, p=.017. Replicates all three main findings of Oaksford and Hahn (2004).
quote: Fallacies, or arguments that seem correct but aren't, have been a longstanding focus of debate.
limits: Student sample, written dialogues, within-subject. Effects of polarity and prior are small (0.15 to 0.26 points on 0-10); reliability is large (2.4 points). Conference paper.
agent_relevance: Source reliability dominates. This supports marking an unverified source in S1 and weighting it, because reliability moves belief the most.

source: Bayindir, Hahn, Oaksford (2005) Experiment 2 (structural variants of negative evidence)
finding: 72 participants rated four structural variants (a positive, b opposite-polarity negative, c, d same-polarity negative). Negative variants were always weaker than positive evidence, but the opposite-polarity negative case still scored clearly above zero. Variant (b) was not always weaker than (d): worse for two topics only.
numbers: Opposite-polarity negative evidence differs from 0: t(71)=9.16, p<.0001, m=3.36, SE=.37. Topic and structural variant effects F(3,217)=35.55 and 19.05, p<.0001; interaction F(9,217)=3.71, p<.0001.
limits: Same lab, same method; no independent replication by another group in my sources. A Turkish dissertation (2012) reportedly found only a reliability effect (per a search snippet, not opened).
agent_relevance: Even 'nobody has disproven it' carries some weight. A hard ban on guesses and absence-of-evidence is too crude; weight them low and keep them marked.

source: Bayindir, Hahn, Oaksford (2005) discussion: burden-of-proof (pragma-dialectics) vs Bayesian explanation of argument from ignorance
finding: The paper contrasts two accounts of 'Ghosts exist because nobody proved they don't'. Pragma-dialectics says it is fallacious because it shifts the burden of proof (Rule 2). The authors say that only labels the problem and does not explain why the ghost case is weak while an inference from many failed side-effect studies is strong.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Competing explanation, argued not tested head to head.
agent_relevance: Burden-of-proof checks are cheap to code (who asserted, who gave support) but need a probability layer to avoid false alarms.

source: Jin, Lalwani, Vaidhya, Shen, Ding et al. (2022) Logical Fallacy Detection (EMNLP Findings), LOGIC and LOGICCLIMATE
finding: First multi-type fallacy detection set and 12-model test. LOGIC has 2,449 items over 13 fallacy types from quiz sites; LOGICCLIMATE has 1,079 climate-news sentences. Zero-shot models were near random. A structure-aware Electra classifier that masks content words and adds the logical form beat the best plain language model.
numbers: Micro-F1 on LOGIC: random 12.02, GPT-3 12.20, GPT-2 13.67, RoBERTa-MNLI 12.22, BART-MNLI 11.05, TARS 8.62; fine-tuned BERT 45.80, DeBERTa 50.29, Electra 53.31, Electra-StructAware 58.77 (+5.46). On LOGICCLIMATE the structure model reached 27.23 (+4.51 over Electra). Class F1: ad populum 79.45, ad hominem 78.65, deductive fallacy 25.81 (lowest). Annotator accuracy above 85%.
limits: Items are textbook examples from quiz sites, so models may learn textbook wording. GPT-3 was prompted only (2022 era). Large drop out of domain.
agent_relevance: Plain prompting of 2022 models found no fallacies. Structure helps modestly. The agent should not rely on a model's bare label for 'is this a fallacy'.

source: Sourati, Prasanna Venkatesh, Deshpande et al. (2023) Robust and explainable identification of logical fallacies in natural language arguments (Knowledge-Based Systems)
finding: Three-stage framework: detection, coarse class, fine class. Case-based (instance and prototype) methods with Electra did best in domain, with augmentation and curriculum learning. Binary detection on BIG-bench was near solved, but fine-grained and out-of-domain scores fell.
numbers: BIG-bench binary F1: random 0.499, NLI Electra 0.995, instance-based 0.997, prototype 0.984, knowledge-injection BERT 0.777. LOGIC in-domain instance-based: coarse F1 82.7%, fine F1 62.7%. LOGIC Climate coarse: instance-based 46.6% vs prototype 57.3%; fine about 24%.
limits: The BIG-bench binary task is too easy (near-perfect scores suggest cue leakage; compare a20). Fine-tuned encoders, not prompted LLMs.
agent_relevance: Detecting 'is there a flaw' is easy on clean sets and hard in the wild; do not trust high benchmark scores.

source: Helwe, Calamai, Paris, Clavel, Suchanek (2024) MAFALDA: a benchmark and comprehensive study of fallacy detection and classification (NAACL)
finding: Unifies four fallacy datasets under one three-level taxonomy (9,745 texts; 200 hand-annotated with 260 fallacy instances and justifications). Disjunctive labels allow several correct answers because annotation is subjective. 13 zero-shot LLMs were tested; humans beat all models. Appeal to emotion was the hardest class for people and models.
numbers: Span-level F1 (Level 0 / 1 / 2): random 0.435/0.061/0.010; GPT-3.5 0.627/0.201/0.138 (best model); Zephyr 7B 0.524/0.192/0.098; LLaMA2-7B beat 13B at levels 0 and 1; average human on a 20-text sample 0.749/0.352/0.186. 28% of spans (65 of 203) have two or more alternative labels. Each of 4 human annotators scored only 0.093-0.144 at Level 2 against the gold standard (the gold standard itself scored 0.186 against them).
limits: Human baseline is only 4 annotators on 20 texts. Zero-shot with basic prompts only; 2023-era models.
agent_relevance: Even humans agree little on the exact fallacy name. The agent should flag 'weak support' and the reason, not insist on one label.

source: Pan, Wu, Li, Luu (2024) Are LLMs good zero-shot fallacy classifiers? (EMNLP)
finding: Zero-shot prompting across seven fallacy sets (Argotario, Reddit, LOGIC, ElecDeb60to20, MAFALDA, Propaganda, COVID). Single-round GPT-4 matched or beat fine-tuned T5 baselines out of domain and on some sets. Multi-round prompts with explicit fallacy analysis helped small models most. Informal vs formal definitions did not change MAFALDA results much for the top model.
numbers: Macro-F1: GPT-4 single-round 78.94 on Argotario and 79.10 on Reddit vs best T5-3B 83.20 and 80.42. On MAFALDA, GPT-4 48.38 (informal definition) and 49.78 (formal); GPT-3.5 31.27 and 27.10; Llama2-13B 22.09 with 27.7% failed outputs. Best multi-round rank: General Fallacy Analysis with Warm Up (4.13 average rank), then zero-shot CoT (4.33).
limits: Many benchmarks are crowd-written or textbook-like. Failed-output rates are high for small models (up to 27.7%).
agent_relevance: A short 'analyse for fallacies first' round beats a bare label for small models. Use as a gated step, only on a signal (G1), and let code count failed outputs.

source: Jeong, Jang, Park (2025) LLMs are better logical fallacy reasoners with counterargument, explanation, goal-aware prompt formulation (NAACL Findings)
finding: Adds three auto-generated context queries to each input: a counterargument, an explanation and a goal. The model scores each query's validity and code ranks them by confidence. Works zero-shot and fine-tuned across 5 domains and 29 fallacy types.
numbers: Claimed gains up to +0.60 Macro-F1 zero-shot and +0.45 fine-tuned. Example table row (Macro-F1/accuracy pairs by dataset): Prompt Ranking 0.35/0.17, 0.84/0.69, 0.45/0.32, 0.71/0.56, 0.63/0.58 vs plain zero-shot 0.32/0.19, 0.60/0.50, 0.40/0.28, 0.36/0.25, 0.18/0.11; zero-shot CoT 0.14/0.08, 0.48/0.39, 0.39/0.23, 0.29/0.11, 0.20/0.13.
limits: Max gains come from single datasets; some datasets improve little (0.32 to 0.35). Zero-shot CoT was worse than plain zero-shot on several sets. GPT and LLaMA series only. Column labels were read from a table layout and may be off.
agent_relevance: A counterargument-first step is a fit for our alternatives operator, and ranking by confidence in code fits G5. Zero-shot CoT can hurt.

source: Li et al. (2024) Reason from fallacy: enhancing LLM logical reasoning through logical fallacy understanding (NAACL Findings)
finding: Builds LFUD (4,020 GPT-4 generated instances, five WHAT/WHY/HOW tasks). Fine-tuning on logic data plus LFUD raised accuracy on four reasoning sets, while adding LOGIC fallacy sentences did not help and sometimes hurt.
numbers: Relative accuracy change vs Origin: LogiQA2.0 LLaMA2-13B 45.55 to 47.90 (+5.16%); Reclor Vicuna-13B 54.40 to 57.00 (+4.78%); FOLIO Vicuna-13B 36.76 to 44.61 (+21.35%). Origin+LOGIC: TaxiNLI LLaMA2-13B 68.54 to 40.60 (-40.76%), LLaMA2-7B LogiQA2.0 -15.79%. Three runs averaged; five models (7B-13B).
limits: Synthetic GPT-4 data and fine-tuning, which we do not do. Gains are for small open models only.
agent_relevance: Teaching fallacy knowledge may help reasoning, but only when the data covers why and how to fix, not just labels.

source: Singh, Pathak, Singh (2026) Fallacy benchmarks measure scheme recognition, not fallacy detection
finding: Valid classes in fallacy benchmarks are the residue of data collection and almost never hold a correct argument that uses the same scheme as a fallacy (e.g. a valid expert appeal). Two annotators found 3 such items in 183 sampled. When such matched valid arguments were built, a classifier flagged them as the source fallacy far more than a control with a different scheme. It had learned the scheme, not whether the critical question was answered.
numbers: Fine-tuned classifier flags 16.6% of CoCoLoFa's native valid class but 58.9% of matched negatives (Reddit-trained: 5.7% to 62.0%). Matched negatives are classified as source type 40.9 points more often than wrong-scheme negatives; wrong-scheme negatives get their own scheme 85.9% of the time and the source type 0.4%. 76.9% of fallacy misses land on 'none' (95% CI 64.8-86.7). Native false-positive rate 3% on CoCoLoFa, 40% Reddit, 52% MAFALDA, 65% Argotario. Appeal to authority matched vs native: 78.8% vs 11.7%. Annotators agreed on 86.3%.
limits: Preprint (Sept 2026), not peer reviewed; constructed items for eight fallacy types; classifiers mostly fine-tuned, with three zero-shot LLM detectors showing the same pattern.
agent_relevance: Key for S1: a flagger for authority or guesses will over-flag valid expert appeals. The agent should check the critical questions (is the expert real, relevant, quoted right), not the surface shape.

source: Payandeh, Pluth, Hosier, Xiao, Gurbani (2023) How susceptible are LLMs to logical fallacies? LOGICOM (arXiv 2308.09853)
finding: Persuader-debater setup with 200 claims from Habernal et al. (2018). The persuader used either logical arguments or fallacious ones (made by a helper agent). Each claim was run three times. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 debaters changed their mind more often under fallacies; GPT-4 was the more susceptible.
numbers: Debater moved from disagree to agree in 16.13% (GPT-3.5) and 20.25% (GPT-4) of cases. Convinced on average by fallacious persuader 37% (GPT-3.5) vs 29% logical; GPT-4 67% fallacious vs 37% logical; in all three runs: GPT-3.5 17% vs 10%, GPT-4 56% vs 37%. Abstract claims 41% (GPT-3.5) and 69% (GPT-4) more often convinced by fallacies. Helper ablation: persuader wins only with the fallacious helper in 10.5% (GPT-3.5) and 0.83% (GPT-4) of claims.
limits: Only two models (2023), one prompt design, three repeats; the 41% and 69% do not match simple ratios of the averages quoted in the text, so treat them as the authors' own measure.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence the model is moved by fallacious input. The agent must not take the other side of a persuasive text at face value (G4/G5).

source: Chen, Greschner, Klinger, Klenk, Eger (2026) Emotionally charged, logically blurred: AI-driven emotional framing impairs human fallacy detection
finding: Eight LLMs rewrote fallacious arguments with emotional framing (enjoyment, fear, sadness, surprise, disgust) while keeping the logic. Prolific workers (US/UK, native English, degree) labelled 1,000 arguments (200 original, 800 framed) for fallacy type and emotion. Humans detected fallacies worse on the framed versions.
numbers: Fallacy detection F1 fell by 14.5% on average (0.380-0.533 vs 0.563 original). Share labelled fallacious dropped from 91% to 86% (5.5% relative). Worst: qwen3-32b with loaded words (0.380); mildest: ds-llama-70b with imagery (0.533). Pre-quiz average 3.81/5. Annotation cost 360 euros.
limits: Five fallacy types only; humans seldom noticed the injected emotion. Emotion matching by models was low. Convincingness rose only slightly.
agent_relevance: Emotive wording in the input makes fallacies harder to spot, for people. The agent's S1 pass should strip tone and restate the claim neutrally before judging support.

source: Zhai et al. (2025) RuozhiBench: evaluating LLMs with logical fallacies and misleading premises
finding: 677 bilingual trick questions with deceptive premises. 17 LLMs from 5 series, open-ended and two-choice formats. The best model was far below humans.
numbers: Best model (Claude-3-haiku) 62% accuracy vs humans above 90%.
limits: Questions are built to trap, so a pass means avoiding the trap, not general fallacy skill. 2025 models.
agent_relevance: Models accept false premises smoothly. Premises should be checked before answering (S1 hygiene).

source: Shen, Yuan, Chen, Wu, Cai, Wu (2026) Truth or sophistry? LoFa: a benchmark for LLM robustness against logical fallacies
finding: Pairs factual questions with fallacious arguments pushing a wrong answer and runs multi-round attacks. LFR@k measures resistance only where the model first knew the answer. Models resisted flaws of reasoning (hasty generalization, slippery slope, circular) better than distraction fallacies (equivocation, straw man) and fabricated authority.
numbers: Llama-3.1 average LFR@3 59.75% (8B), 70.38% (70B), 77.17% (405B). Llama-3.1-405B LFR@3: 29.4% vs equivocation, 57.0% vs straw man. GPT-4: 39.2% LFR@3 vs fabricated authority cues. Closed models tested May-July 2025 via API; results averaged over three runs.
limits: Attackers are LLM-generated fallacies, so the mix may differ from human fallacies. The authors suggest RLHF context adherence causes the authority deference (untested).
agent_relevance: Fabricated authority is a weak spot. This directly supports putting appeals to authority in a marked block that cannot change the answer without a check (S1).

source: Ballon et al. (2026) Big-Big-SycoBench: sycophancy through valid vs invalid arguments
finding: 450 text artefacts, 5,400 arguments for raising or lowering a quality score, valid or invalid; invalid ones use authority, consensus, emotion, bare assertion. A revision counts only if above the model's own twenty-run noise. Models differ widely in following invalid pressure while staying responsive to valid criticism.
numbers: Invalid-argument following 0.15% (GPT-6 Astra), 9.1% (GLM-5.3), 13.3% (Kimi K3), 19.7% (Grok 4.7), 21.9% (GPT-5.5), 28.3% (GPT-5.6 Terra), 37.7% (GPT-5.6 Luna), 56.8% (GPT-5), 94.6% (GPT-4o). Valid following 88-95% for seven of ten models; GPT-4o 89.0% valid vs 94.6% invalid. Contrarian moves below 0.2%. Annotators accepted labels 94.1%.
limits: Preprint (Oct 2026); scores text quality, not truth. Opus 5.5 was run on a 100-artefact subset only (32.2% valid, 0.8% invalid).
agent_relevance: Discernment is possible and varies by model, so we should measure it for our own model and not assume. Authority and consensus cues move many models.

source: Carrillo et al. (2026) Talk2AI: LLM persuasion and fallacies in longitudinal conversations (arXiv 2604.16935)
finding: 770 participants held structured chats with one of four LLMs on polarising topics: 3,080 conversations, over 60,000 turns. NLP analysis found fallacious reasoning in about 1 of every 6 quips, by both humans and LLMs.
numbers: 770 participants; 3,080 conversations; more than 60,000 turns; fallacy rate about 1 in 6 turns. Perceived humanness R2=0.44, opinion change R2=0.34, conviction R2=0.26.
limits: The fallacy labelling is automatic (NLP), with the error rate of such detectors (see a14, a16, a20). Not a causal test of fallacy effects.
agent_relevance: LLM outputs themselves contain fallacies at a notable rate. The agent should run its own candidate text through the same support check.

source: Huang et al. (2026) ForEx: formal verification of LLM explanations in logical fallacy detection (arXiv 2606.21867)
finding: Translates LLM fallacy explanations into Lean4 and checks derivability from the encoded premises, not the validity of the original argument. Most explanations verify formally, yet labels barely match humans.
numbers: Over 90% of LLM outputs translated into chains that pass verification; agreement with human labels about 20% on LOGIC-Climate.
limits: Verification certifies only that the translated rationale is self-consistent, not that it is faithful or right.
agent_relevance: A checkable rationale is not a correct one (G3). A pass on internal consistency needs an outside test.

source: Yeh et al. (2024) CoCoLoFa: news comments with common logical fallacies written by LLM-assisted crowds
finding: Largest English fallacy set at the time: 7,706 comments on 648 news articles, written by 143 crowd workers with an LLM writing helper; experts rated quality and label validity high. Fine-tuned BERT-type models scored high in domain and lost ground on other sets.
numbers: Fine-tuned detection F1=0.86, classification F1=0.87 on its own test set; 0.05 lower on Reddit and 0.13 lower on another set (0.73 vs 0.86). Models trained on other sets scored only 0.19 and 0.09 F1 on CoCoLoFa in one comparison.
limits: Comments are written on request to show a fallacy, so they may be cleaner than real ones. Singh et al. (a20) find its native valid class easy.
agent_relevance: Training and test data written to order inflate scores; expect weaker flagging on real inputs.

source: Gajewska, Budzynska, Chudziak (2026) Benchmarking argumentative behaviour of LLMs: defences against character attacks (arXiv 2609.28673)
finding: Tests on the ElecDeb60to16-fallacy corpus whether LLMs use and answer ad hominem like human debaters. Humans mix logical rebuttals with ethotic counterattacks; LLMs almost only use logical defence. Authors argue ad hominem has legitimate roles when character is the issue, and that safety tuning narrows the move set.
numbers: Humans: logical rebuttals 59%, ethotic counterattacks 32%, undercutters 9%. LLMs: logical defences 67-76%, ethotic counterattacks 15-17% (about half the human rate); undercutters 18% vs 9% in one comparison.
limits: One corpus of US presidential debates; the claim about safety tuning is the authors' hypothesis, not tested.
agent_relevance: Supports Walton's view that ad hominem can be a valid scheme. The agent should ask whether source character is relevant to the claim, not ban it.

source: Kanke (2026) DeflectBench: rhetorical fallacy generation in LLMs (arXiv 2608.26119)
finding: 23,990 generations from four frontier models: whataboutism, ad hominem, red herring over 80 claims and seven prompt framings. Refusal depends on request framing, not claim content. An educational debate coach frame drops refusal near zero, usually with the fallacy named.
numbers: Refusal varies by only 11 points across 80 claims; one frame change swings within-model refusal by nearly 100 points; changing fallacy type swings it by over 80 points.
limits: Abstract and first page read; four models only.
agent_relevance: Models can produce fallacies on request, so a fallacy-flagging step has to also check our own drafts, not only inputs.
